extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, policymakers, and readers interested in public opinion, political psychology, and media effects
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for understanding and evaluating how public opinion is formed, distorted, and communicated — focusing on language, attention, emotional bias, environment, and stereotypes, and the role of media. Useful for analysts, journalists, and students assessing the reliability and quality of public beliefs and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words-as-tokens-of-value / word-exchange fluctuations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Words, like money, are tokens of value. They represent meaning, therefore, and just as money, their representative value goes up and down... For there is a war fluctuation on word exchanges as well as on money exchanges."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading foreign-language press or cross-cultural discourse, mentally 'convert' evaluative words rather than taking them at face value; recognise that nuance and connotation change over time and with circumstance (e.g., wartime inflation of certain terms). Examples: how 'etonnant' or 'awful' carry different historical weights; expressions such as 'a distinguished scholar' translate into richer or inflated phrases in other languages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words-evoke-composite-images that shape opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: "To them the words so acquired are the cue for a whole train of ideas on which ultimately a vote of untold consequences may be based."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that single words (e.g., 'Mexico', 'Japan', 'alien') evoke composite, often stereotyped images that supply most of the data on which people form opinions. Analysts should account for these mental images when interpreting public attitudes because the word triggers a network of associations rather than a neutral fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity: ability to dissociate superficial analogies and attend to differences
rubrics_metrics.description: "The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety is lucidity of mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments and opinions by checking whether the thinker separates crude analogies and attends to genuine differences (illustrated by contrasts: infant vs botanist, Union League member vs sophisticated anarchist). High-quality public reasoning shows discrimination between superficially similar items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention and discrimination are flattened by fatigue and distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Slight mental fatigue, an inner disturbance of attention or an external distraction, tend to 'flatten' the quality of the response... If the beat of a metronome will depress intelligence, what do eight or twelve hours of noise... do to the political judgments formed on the basis of newspapers read in street-cars and subways?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the informational conditions under which opinions are formed: noisy, crowded, and hurried environments reduce people's ability to discriminate and reason. Policy implications include supporting solitude, shorter workdays, and environments that permit sustained attention when informed judgment is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional conflicts and unconscious complexes distort reading and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "The speed, the accuracy, and the intellectual quality of association is deranged by what we are taught to call emotional conflicts... Obviously our public opinion is in intermittent contact with complexes of all sorts; with ambition and economic interest, personal animosity, racial prejudice, class feeling and what not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating opinions or reports, factor in likely emotional investments and unconscious motives (ambition, prejudice, class interests). Emotional conflicts can produce delayed, inconsistent, or biased responses measurable even in brief association tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience heterogeneity and tailoring appeals (broad vs narrow appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A 'broad appeal' takes account of the quality of association, and is made to those susceptibilities which are widely distributed. A 'narrow' or a 'special' appeal is one made to those susceptibilities which are uncommon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and evaluate persuasive messages according to the 'psychic level' of audiences: broad appeals target widely shared, shallow susceptibilities; narrow appeals target specialized or rare susceptibilities. Media and publishers choose formats (e.g., imagery) that match the desired psychic level for circulation or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to access and information distortion (censorship, language poverty, social barriers)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus the environment with which our public opinions deal is refracted in many ways, by censorship and privacy at the source, by physical and social barriers at the other end, by scanty attention, by the poverty of language, by distraction, by unconscious constellations of feeling..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the reliability or fairness of public opinion, systematically account for barriers that refract information flow — source censorship, social constraints on expression, limited vocabulary, and distributional impediments. These structural factors combine to produce systematic distortions in public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes precede perception: 'we define first and then see'
rubrics_metrics.description: "For the most part we do not first see, and then define, we define first and then see."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that cultural and conceptual categories shape perception before observation; people's background definitions determine what they notice. Evaluations of testimony or reporting should ask what preexisting categories guided the observer's perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes preempt and contaminate eyewitness and observer reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental evidence: many trained observers reported scenes that had not occurred — "In thirty-four out of the forty observers the stereotypes preempted at least one-tenth of the scene."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat eyewitness and immediate reports with caution: stereotyped expectations can fill in or invent details. Use corroboration, steps to recover original impressions, and awareness of common stereotype-driven errors when assessing reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appraise the minds that filtered information, not just the information itself
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we cannot fully understand the acts of other people, until we know what they think they know, then in order to do justice we have to appraise not only the information which has been at their disposal, but the minds through which they have filtered it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should evaluate the cognitive and cultural filters of sources (education, exposure to stereotypes, local conventions) as part of interpreting statements or actions. Example: 'Americanization' changes vision as much as information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold stereotypes lightly and trace their historical origins
rubrics_metrics.description: "What matters is the character of the stereotypes, and the gullibility with which we employ them... we tend... to hold them lightly, to modify them gladly. We tend, also, to realize more and more clearly when our ideas started, where they started, how they came to us... All useful history is antiseptic in this fashion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice reflexivity about received images and classifications: trace where a stereotype originated (books, films, traditions) and be willing to revise it. Historical investigation is a corrective that reduces the dogmatic force of stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and visual representations strongly build and fix stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Photographs have the kind of authority over imagination to-day, which the printed word had yesterday... On the screen the whole process of observing, describing, reporting, and then imagining, has been accomplished for you... the Birth of a Nation... takes vivid shape when you see the film."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the outsized role of photographs and films in forming durable public images; visual media can create vivid, persistent stereotypes that are resistant to later factual correction. When assessing public beliefs, identify influential media portrayals and their likely distortive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of stereotypes: necessary heuristic but source of error
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is economy in this. For the attempt to see all things freshly and in detail... is exhausting, and among busy affairs practically out of the question."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that stereotyping is an adaptive economy of attention — it allows rapid cognition in complex environments — but weigh its efficiency against the risk of error. Good practice balances heuristic use of types with targeted efforts at individualized understanding where stakes are high.
